Session 1 · 1.1 What a programming language is · 1/3Book ↗

From human ideas to machine instructions

  • Processors understand only machine code: numbers
  • A programming language is a human-readable notation with strict grammar (syntax)
  • What the programmer writes is source code
  • Something must translate source code into machine code
Session 1 · 1.1 What a programming language is · 2/3Book ↗

Two ways to translate

  • Compiler: translate the whole program ahead of time into an executable. Fast; tied to one platform. C, C++, Rust, Go, Swift
  • Interpreter: carry out the source code on the spot. Portable; slower. Python, JavaScript, Ruby
  • Analogy: a published translation versus a live interpreter in the room
Session 1 · 1.1 What a programming language is · 3/3Book ↗

Language, library, framework

  • Language: the notation itself (Python)
  • Library: ready-made code for one job (send email, draw a chart)
  • Framework: the skeleton of a whole kind of application (Flask, React)
  • Hundreds of languages exist because each makes one kind of work easier at the cost of another
In the age of AI: syntax is the part AI has fully absorbed. The trade-offs below have not gone away.
Session 1 · 1.2 Fit for purpose · 1/3Book ↗

Was the language built for the job?

  • General-purpose languages can write almost anything: Python, JavaScript, Java, C#, C++, Go, Rust
  • Domain-specific languages do one thing superbly: SQL (database questions), HTML (structure), CSS (style)
  • Nobody writes a website in SQL: it cannot draw a button, react to a click, or send an email
Session 1 · 1.2 Fit for purpose · 2/3Book ↗

Where each language lives

  • Browser: only JavaScript. Database: only SQL
  • The server admits almost anything: that is the real choice
Session 1 · 1.2 Fit for purpose · 3/3Book ↗

A product is never one language

  • Typical web product: HTML + CSS + JavaScript in the browser, Python (or JS) on the server, SQL in the database
  • Add Swift and Kotlin for native phone apps
  • "Choosing a language" really means choosing the back-end language and the mobile strategy
In the age of AI: fit for purpose is unchanged. Using several languages in one product is cheaper than it was.
Session 1 · 1.3 Popularity, maturity, and community · 1/2Book ↗

A language is a community, not just a notation

  • Hiring: millions of developers versus a few thousand
  • Answers: every problem in a popular language has been solved publicly
  • Longevity: COBOL from the 1970s still runs banks; who maintains it now?
  • Security: many eyes find and fix flaws quickly
  • Tooling: editors, testing, hosting support the popular languages first
Session 1 · 1.3 Popularity, maturity, and community · 2/2Book ↗

The mainstream, and the caution about the new

  • Mainstream today: Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, C#, C/C++, Go, SQL; Rust, Swift, Kotlin in their niches
  • A brand-new language may be better designed and still be the wrong choice: few libraries, breaking changes, unproven survival
  • Most successful languages needed ten years to become safe bets
In the age of AI: popularity matters MORE. AI learns from public code, so mainstream, stable languages get the best help.
Session 1 · 1.4 The ecosystem: packages and libraries · 1/2Book ↗

Nobody writes it from scratch

  • Email, spreadsheets, payments, images, charts: someone already wrote it and published it free
  • The ecosystem = the libraries plus the tools to find and install them
  • Package manager: pip (Python), npm (JavaScript). "We added a dependency"
  • Almost all of it is open source, which is also a supply chain to watch
Session 1 · 1.4 The ecosystem: packages and libraries · 2/2Book ↗

The ecosystem steers the choice

If the product is mostly about…The ecosystem pulls toward
AI, machine learning, dataPython
Rich interactive web front endJavaScript / TypeScript
Conventional web back endPython, JavaScript, Ruby, Java, C#, Go
Enterprise integrationJava, C#
GamesC# (Unity), C++ (Unreal)
Native phone appSwift / Kotlin
In the age of AI: ecosystems matter as much as ever. Watch for hallucinated packages that do not exist.
Session 1 · 1.5 Speed and memory · 1/2Book ↗

The fastest language is usually the wrong question

  • Compiled languages can be 10 to 100 times faster than Python at raw computation
  • But most business apps wait (database, network, disk); they do not compute
  • Developer time costs far more than machine time
  • Python's AI libraries are C inside: "Python is slow" and "Python runs AI" are both true
Session 1 · 1.5 Speed and memory · 2/2Book ↗

When performance genuinely decides

SituationWhyTypical choice
Embedded devices, wearablesKilobytes of memory, a batteryC, C++, Rust
Games, video16 ms per frameC++, C#, Rust
Trading, real-time controlMicroseconds are money or safetyC++, Rust
Very large services10× efficiency = thousands of serversGo, Rust, Java
Mobile appsBattery and memory limitsSwift, Kotlin
Build in the productive language, measure, then rewrite only the proven hot spot. In the age of AI that last step is cheap.
Session 1 · 1.6 Platforms and portability · 1/4Book ↗

A platform is processor + operating system

  • Processor families: x86 (Intel, AMD) and ARM (phones, Apple silicon, new servers)
  • Operating systems: Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android
  • Machine code for one platform is gibberish to another
  • Every extra platform is another version to build, test, and support
Session 1 · 1.6 Platforms and portability · 2/4Book ↗

Three ways to reach three platforms

Session 1 · 1.6 Platforms and portability · 3/4Book ↗

Recompile, virtual machine, or interpret

  • Recompile per platform (C, C++, Rust): fastest; one build per platform. Apple's 2020 move to ARM forced every Mac app to be rebuilt
  • Compile once to bytecode (Java, Kotlin, C#): "write once, run anywhere" on a virtual machine
  • Interpret the source (Python, JavaScript): ship the file itself. JavaScript's interpreter is in every browser, so the web is the most portable platform ever
Session 1 · 1.6 Platforms and portability · 4/4Book ↗

Phones are the special case

  • Apple prefers Swift; Google prefers Kotlin. Both compiled for the phone
  • The best app on both platforms means writing it twice
  • Cross-platform frameworks (React Native, Flutter) produce both from one codebase, with some loss of polish
  • Electron does the same for desktop (Slack, VS Code, Discord)
In the age of AI: porting code between platforms is cheaper. Testing on every real device is not.
Session 1 · 1.7 Making the decision in the age of AI · 1/2Book ↗

How each factor shifts

FactorBefore AIWith AI assistance
Fit for purposeDecisiveUnchanged
Popularity and maturityHighHigher: AI quality tracks public code
EcosystemHighUnchanged to higher; verify packages
Speed and memoryDecisive in a few domainsSame domains; elsewhere lower
PlatformsHigh (duplicated work)Lower for writing; same for testing
Your own familiarityOften decisiveLower, but you still review the code
Session 1 · 1.7 Making the decision in the age of AI · 2/2Book ↗

Three conclusions

  • Choose mainstream. Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, SQL; Java or C# when the enterprise requires; Swift and Kotlin for native mobile
  • Optimise for readability. When AI writes the code, the human's job is reading it
  • The language is rarely the risk. Products fail on requirements, data models, and security, not Python versus Go
This module uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript in the browser; Python on the server; SQL in the database.
